lessons.title: Silver: The Precious Metal With an Industrial Side

children.text: In March 2020, as COVID lockdowns spread, silver crashed to around $12 an ounce. Factories were shutting, and silver is an industrial metal. By August 2020, it had climbed to around $29, far outpacing gold's rally over the same months. Silver is a precious metal, bought as coins, jewellery and payal in homes across India. It is also an industrial raw material that goes into solar panels, electronics and vehicles. By the end of this lesson you will understand silver's dual personality, what drives its demand and supply, how to use the gold-silver ratio, and why silver swings much harder than gold in both directions.

body.text: Silver behaves like gold when fear and interest rates dominate, and like an industrial metal when the global economy dominates. That split personality is why it tends to rise faster than gold in good times and fall harder in bad times.

children.text: Two Metals in One
More than half of the world's silver demand comes from industry. The rest comes from the same kinds of buyers as gold: jewellery, coins and bars, and silverware.

children.text: The Industrial Side: Solar, Electronics and Vehicles
Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal. That makes it hard to replace in many applications.
Solar panels.
Silver paste is used in photovoltaic cells, and the global solar build-out has made this one of the fastest-growing sources of silver demand.
Electronics and electrical parts.
Switches, contacts, circuit boards and connectors in everything from phones to power grids.
Vehicles.
Modern cars use silver in electrical systems, and electric vehicles tend to use more.
Brazing, soldering and other uses.
Joining metals in air conditioners, plumbing and industrial equipment.

body.text: Because industrial buyers use silver in small quantities per product, many are not very sensitive to price in the short run. A solar manufacturer will not stop production because silver rose 10%. But over the long run, high prices push manufacturers to thrift, using less silver per cell, which can cap demand growth.

children.text: The Supply Side: Silver Is Mostly a By-Product

markDefs.definition: A secondary product recovered while mining or refining something else. Most silver is recovered while mining lead, zinc, copper or gold.

children.text: Here is the most important supply fact about silver: most of it is not mined for its own sake. Roughly 70% of mined silver comes as a
by-product
of mining lead, zinc, copper and gold.

That makes silver supply stubborn. If silver prices double, a zinc miner does not dig more zinc just to get more silver, because silver is a small part of its revenue. India's own Hindustan Zinc, part of the Vedanta group, is one of the world's large silver producers precisely because of its zinc and lead mines in Rajasthan.

body.title: Why supply is stubborn
body.textWithBlank: Roughly 70% of the world's mined silver is produced as a ___ of mining lead, zinc, copper and gold.
body.explanation: Because most silver comes out of mines run for other metals, higher silver prices do not quickly bring more supply. That is one reason silver prices can spike hard when demand jumps.

children.text: Why Silver Swings Harder Than Gold

Silver's market is far smaller than gold's in value, its industrial demand rises and falls with the economy, and speculative money moves in and out quickly. Put together, silver tends to amplify gold's moves.

body.text: Silver's higher volatility applies directly to your MCX position. A 3% day in silver is ordinary. On one lot of Silver (30 kg) at ₹1,20,000 per kg, a 3% move is ₹3,600 per kg, or ₹1,08,000 on the lot. Beginners who are drawn to silver because a kilogram "costs less than 10 grams of gold" often underestimate this.

body.title: A normal silver day on Silver Mini
body.prompt: MCX Silver Mini covers 5 kg and is quoted in ₹ per kg. Silver is at ₹1,20,000 per kg and falls 3% in a day. What is the loss on one long lot, in rupees? Enter the loss as a negative number.
body.explanation: 3% of ₹1,20,000 = ₹3,600 per kg. × 5 kg = ₹18,000 loss on one Silver Mini lot. On the 30 kg Silver lot, the same move would cost ₹1,08,000.

children.text: The Gold-Silver Ratio

markDefs.definition: The number of units of silver it takes to buy one unit of gold by weight. Calculated as the gold price divided by the silver price, in the same currency and weight unit.

children.text: Traders compare the two metals using the
gold-silver ratio
: how many ounces of silver it takes to buy one ounce of gold.

body.latex: \text{Gold-silver ratio} = \frac{\text{Gold price per unit weight}}{\text{Silver price per same unit weight}}
body.caption: With MCX prices: (gold ₹ per 10 grams × 100) ÷ silver ₹ per kg, since both then refer to 1 kg.

body.title: Gold-silver ratio at selected points (approximate)
body.yAxisLabel: Ounces of silver per ounce of gold

children.text: When silver outperforms, as it did into its 2011 peak, the ratio falls. When silver underperforms, as it did in the March 2020 panic, the ratio rises. A reading above 120 in March 2020 was an extreme, and it fell back sharply as silver rebounded.

body.title: Calculate the ratio from MCX prices
body.prompt: MCX Gold is ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams and MCX Silver is ₹1,20,000 per kg. What is the gold-silver ratio, rounded to one decimal place?
body.explanation: Gold per kg = ₹1,00,000 × 100 = ₹1,00,00,000. Divide by silver per kg: ₹1,00,00,000 ÷ ₹1,20,000 = 83.3. It takes about 83 kg of silver to buy 1 kg of gold.

body.title: Why the ratio is a lens, not a trading signal

children.text: It is tempting to say "the ratio is high, so silver must be cheap." Be careful.
There is no fixed "correct" ratio. It has spent long periods anywhere from the 30s to above 100.
A high ratio can stay high, or climb higher, for years if industrial demand is weak or central banks keep buying gold but not silver.
Trading the ratio usually means going long one metal and short the other, which carries two sets of margins, rollovers and risks.
Use the ratio to understand relative value and to frame questions, then check the underlying drivers before acting.
Silver in India

India is one of the world's largest silver consumers and imports most of what it uses. Demand comes from jewellery and payal, puja items and utensils, silver coins bought at Dhanteras and Diwali, and industry. Clusters such as Rajkot are known for silver jewellery manufacturing. Like gold, Indian silver prices add the rupee, import duty and 3% GST on top of the international price, and the July 2024 Budget cut customs duty on silver from 15% to 6%, the same as gold.
MCX contracts.
Silver (30 kg), Silver Mini (5 kg) and Silver Micro (1 kg) let traders choose their size, all quoted in ₹ per kg.
Silver ETFs.
After SEBI permitted silver ETFs, the first launched in India in early 2022, giving investors demat-based silver without storage worries.
Physical silver.
Coins, bars and articles remain popular, but come with purity checks, making charges on articles and resale discounts. The next lesson compares every route.

body.title: Where silver and gold part ways
body.question: Which news is most likely to hurt silver noticeably more than gold?
options: Central banks announce record gold purchases
Global manufacturing data points to a sharp slowdown, including in solar installations
body.explanation: A manufacturing slowdown hits silver's industrial demand, which gold barely has. A stronger dollar tends to weigh on both, central bank buying mainly supports gold, and falling real yields tend to support both.

body.title: The ratio trade
body.scenario: Deepak, a 38-year-old trader in Hyderabad, reads that the gold-silver ratio is 90, well above what he believes is a long-run average of about 65. He plans to put his entire ₹5,00,000 trading capital into margin for 2 lots of Silver (30 kg each) on MCX, saying "the ratio has to come back to 65, and silver will explode."
body.prompt: What is sound in Deepak's thinking, and what are the risks in his plan?
body.modelAnswer:
What is sound: a high ratio does mean silver has underperformed gold, and historically extreme readings have sometimes reversed sharply, as in 2020.

The risks:
1. "Has to" is wrong. The ratio has no fixed average it must return to, and it can stay high for years.
2. The ratio can fall because gold drops, not because silver rises. A long silver position could still lose money if both metals fall.
3. Size. Two 30 kg lots at ₹1,20,000 per kg are worth ₹72,00,000. A 3% move is ₹2,16,000, over 40% of his capital, and silver moves 3% routinely. Using all his capital as margin leaves no buffer for MTM losses or margin increases.
4. A true ratio trade would pair long silver with short gold in matching value. His plan is simply a leveraged long silver bet.

Better: size the position so a realistic adverse move costs a small share of capital, consider Silver Mini or Micro, set an exit level in advance, and treat the ratio as one input rather than a guarantee.

points: Silver is both a precious metal and an industrial metal, with industry making up more than half of demand.
Solar panels, electronics and vehicles are key industrial uses, so silver responds to global growth in a way gold does not.
About 70% of silver is mined as a by-product, so supply responds slowly to price.
Silver typically falls harder and rises faster than gold, as the 2011 to 2015 and 2020 episodes showed.
The gold-silver ratio measures relative value; it is a useful lens, not a guarantee of reversion.
